Act I — Neuroscience
This is not a behavior problem. This is a nervous system speaking.
The Neuroscience
Self-hitting activates the proprioceptive system — the body's internal GPS that tells the brain where limbs are in space. When proprioceptive input is insufficient, the child's nervous system drives impact-seeking behavior to generate the deep pressure and joint compression it craves.
Self-hitting may also activate endogenous opioid release — the brain's own pain-management system produces a calming effect post-impact, creating a neurobiological reinforcement loop that makes the behavior difficult to extinguish without replacing the underlying sensory reward.
The amygdala in children with dysregulation differences often reaches threshold faster. Hitting can interrupt an overloaded amygdala state by introducing a competing, intense sensory input.
Plain English
  • Their body is craving deep pressure input — like a hunger signal, but sensory
  • Hitting provides the intense joint compression their nervous system needs
  • Sometimes it's communication: "I'm overwhelmed, I can't say it with words"
  • Sometimes it's emotion regulation: the impact interrupts an internal storm
  • Sometimes it's automatic — habitual, like a stim — not intentional harm

"This is a wiring difference, not a behavior choice. Your child is not trying to hurt themselves. They are trying to survive a nervous system that hasn't been given the tools it needs yet." — Pinnacle NeuroDev + OT Consortium

Act II — Learn
D-404: Function-Based Self-Hitting Intervention — 9 Materials Approach
Parent-Friendly Alias: "Giving Your Child Somewhere Else for It to Go"
Self-hitting (clinical: Self-Injurious Behavior — SIB, self-directed type) refers to repetitive behavior in which a child strikes their own body — head, face, limbs — with hands, fists, or against surfaces. This behavior serves specific functions: sensory regulation, emotional regulation, communication, or automatic reinforcement.
The 9 Materials approach provides replacement pathways — materials that meet the same underlying need more safely. The goal is not suppression but substitution: giving the nervous system, the communication system, and the emotional system better tools.

Act II — Disciplines
This technique crosses every therapy boundary — because the child doesn't organize by therapy type.
ABA / BCBA (Primary Lead)
Conducts Functional Behavior Assessment to determine WHY the hitting occurs. Designs function-based intervention: replacement behaviors, reinforcement schedules, extinction protocols, and data collection. FCT is the gold standard for communicatively-motivated SIB.
Occupational Therapy (OT)
Evaluates sensory processing profile. Determines whether hitting is proprioceptive-seeking, overload-escape, or underload-stimulation. Prescribes sensory diet, deep pressure tools, and environmental modifications. Wilbarger Protocol for severe dysregulation.
Speech-Language Pathology (SLP)
Assesses communication function of hitting. Designs AAC system (PECS, communication boards, SGD devices). Teaches functional alternatives: "help," "break," "want," "frustrated." Communicative competence reduces communicatively-motivated SIB.
Special Education (SpEd)
Implements visual supports, schedules, first-then boards, and classroom modifications. Trains school staff on consistent response protocols. Ensures IEP/504 includes SIB intervention plan.
NeuroDev Pediatrics
Rules out medical causes: ear infections, dental pain, GI distress, migraines, seizures. Assesses medication. Provides diagnostic clarity. Medical clearance before behavioral intervention.

Act II — Material 1
Material 1: Deep Pressure Tools
Canon Category: Sensory Regulation / Deep Pressure
Deep pressure tools are often the first and most impactful material to introduce. Weighted blankets (approximately 10% of the child's body weight), compression vests, weighted lap pads, and body socks all deliver the proprioceptive input the child's nervous system is seeking through self-hitting. These tools work proactively — offered throughout the day before the hitting urge builds — rather than only during crisis moments.
What to Get
Weighted blankets, compression vests, weighted lap pads, body socks. Search Amazon.in: "weighted blanket for kids autism therapy"
Price Range
₹800–4,000 | Clinical-grade tools available through OT suppliers
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Rice-filled fabric tube as lap snake; firm pillow "burrito roll"; tight lycra t-shirt as compression layer
Safety Note
~10% of body weight maximum. Never use on children who cannot remove them independently. Never use during sleep.
Act II — Material 2
Material 2: Safe Hitting Alternatives
Canon Category: Impact / Proprioceptive Alternatives
When a child's nervous system is seeking the intense sensation of impact, the goal is not to eliminate that need — it is to redirect it to a safe surface. Hitting pillows, crash pads, child-sized punching bags, drum pads, and bop bags all provide the joint compression and impact sensation that self-hitting delivers, but without injury risk. The key is placement: the safe hitting target must be located exactly where the hitting usually occurs. A pillow across the room does not work.
What to Get
Hitting pillows, crash pads, punching bags (child-sized), drum pads, bop bags. Search Amazon.in: "kids punching bag therapy pillow"
Price Range
₹500–3,000 depending on size and material
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Designated sofa cushion labeled "my hitting pillow"; stacked old blankets as crash pad; cardboard box as drum target
Placement Rule
Position the hitting alternative within arm's reach of where hitting typically occurs — not across the room. Accessibility determines use.
Act II — Material 3
Material 3: AAC / Communication Systems
Canon Category: Communication Tools
When self-hitting is communicative in function — expressing frustration, requesting a break, protesting a demand — the most powerful intervention is giving the child a more effective way to communicate. PECS cards, communication boards, SGD apps, and visual request cards teach the child that a card, a sign, or a symbol produces the outcome faster and more reliably than hitting ever did. Every time you honor a communicative alternative immediately, you are teaching that language works.
What to Get
PECS cards, communication boards, SGD apps (Proloquo2Go, Snap Core), visual request cards. Search Amazon.in: "PECS communication cards autism"
Price Range
₹200–15,000 | Free apps available for basic AAC support
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Printed or drawn picture cards, laminated. Four essential cards: HELP / BREAK / WANT / STOP
Critical Rule
When your child uses their communication system — honor it IMMEDIATELY. Every delayed response teaches hitting is the more reliable language.
Act II — Material 4
Material 4: Protective Gear
Canon Category: Protective Equipment
Protective gear is a bridge tool — it prevents injury while the alternative materials and communication systems are being learned. It is not the end goal; it is the safety net that allows intervention to proceed without the risk of harm during the learning period. Soft-shell protective helmets, padded gloves, arm guards, and wrist padding create a physical buffer that gives you the time and space to implement the other eight materials consistently.
What to Get
Soft-shell protective helmets, padded gloves, arm guards, wrist padding. Search Amazon.in: "protective helmet autism self-injury child"
Price Range
₹1,000–8,000 | Clinical-grade required for severe head-banging
DIY Alternative
Padded cycling helmet; sweatband on wrist; thick cotton wristbands — for mild presentations only
Non-Negotiable Note
Severe head-banging with injury risk requires a professional protective helmet — not a DIY version. Seek OT guidance on correct fitting.
Act II — Material 5
Material 5: Sensory Modulation Tools
Canon Category: Sensory Regulation
Sensory modulation tools address the broader sensory regulatory needs that contribute to hitting — not just the proprioceptive demand, but oral sensory seeking, tactile regulation, auditory overwhelm, and general arousal modulation. Fidgets, chewelry, vibrating sensory tools, therapy brushes, and noise-canceling headphones work across multiple sensory channels to help the child maintain a regulated state so that the hitting threshold is never reached. These are proactive, throughout-the-day tools.
What to Get
Fidgets, chewelry, vibrating sensory tools, therapy brushes, noise-canceling headphones. Search Amazon.in: "chewelry sensory fidget autism child"
Price Range
₹300–2,500 depending on tool type
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Dried rice in sealed zip bag; rubber band ball; rolled towel for squeezing; household items for tactile exploration
Safety Note
Chewelry must be size-appropriate. Supervise during use. Replace when damaged or showing wear.
Act II — Material 6
Material 6: Emotional Regulation Visuals
Canon Category: Emotional Regulation / Visual Supports
When self-hitting is emotionally driven — frustration, disappointment, overwhelm — emotion regulation visuals give the child the vocabulary to name what is happening internally. Feelings charts, Zones of Regulation visuals, emotion thermometers, and calm-down sequence cards externalize the child's internal emotional state so it can be acknowledged, named, and responded to. Naming an emotion is the first step to regulating it. These visuals also give parents a shared language: "You're in the red zone. Let's find a yellow tool."
What to Get
Feelings charts, Zones of Regulation visuals, emotion thermometers, calm-down sequence cards. Search Amazon.in: "zones of regulation feelings chart kids"
Price Range
₹200–1,200 | Many free printable versions available online
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Drawn emoji faces on index cards; hand-drawn thermometer on paper — laminate with tape for durability
Usage Tip
No quiz, no demand. Simply name: "This face is frustrated — like when something is hard." Repeat daily across neutral moments, not only during crisis.
Act II — Material 7
Material 7: Environmental Padding
Canon Category: Environmental Safety / Padding
Environmental padding transforms the physical space into a therapeutic container — one where even during a hitting episode, the risk of serious injury is dramatically reduced. Foam wall panels, floor gym mats, corner guards, foam floor tiles, and crash mats reduce impact surfaces and create soft landing zones. This environmental layer is particularly essential for children who also head-bang or fall to the floor during episodes. It is also psychologically important: a safer space allows parents to respond more calmly instead of from panic.
What to Get
Foam wall panels, floor gym mats, corner guards, foam floor tiles, crash mats. Search Amazon.in: "foam floor mat corner guards child safety padding"
Price Range
₹500–5,000 depending on room coverage needed
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Old cushions against walls; folded blankets at floor impact zones; pool noodles on furniture edges secured with tape
Setup Note
Ensure padding does not create new fall hazards or restrict movement. Leave clear pathways through the space.
Act II — Material 8
Material 8: Calming & Co-Regulation Tools
Canon Category: Calming Tools
Co-regulation — the process of a calm caregiver helping regulate a dysregulated child — is one of the most evidence-supported interventions in pediatric behavioral science. Calming tools create the physical environment for that process: a calm-down corner setup, calming music system, white noise machines, a rocking chair, and weighted comfort items all help shift the child's nervous system from fight-or-flight toward a regulated state. These tools are most effective when pre-established — the child visits the calm corner during good moments, not only during crisis.
What to Get
Calm-down corner setup, calming music system, white noise machines, rocking chair, weighted comfort items
Price Range
₹300–4,000 | Many components cost nothing if repurposed from existing home items
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Free white noise app; floor fan; familiar music playlist; blanket fort; quiet corner with one preferred comfort item
Pinnacle Canon Products
Animal Soft Toys ₹425 — comfort and co-regulation support | Rosette Reward Jar ₹589 for reinforcement
Act II — Material 9
Material 9: FBA / Data Tracking Tools
Canon Category: Assessment / Data Systems
Data is the material that makes all other materials work better. Without tracking, you are guessing. With tracking, you are doing clinical science. ABC data sheets, behavior tracking apps, trigger logs, pattern charts, and sensory checklists allow you to identify exactly when hitting occurs, what precedes it (antecedent), what follows it (consequence), and which alternatives are gaining traction. After 1–2 weeks of consistent data, patterns emerge that will tell you which of the nine materials to prioritize for your specific child.

ABC data sheets, behavior tracking apps, trigger logs, pattern charts, sensory checklists. Free download: pinnacleblooms.org/resources
Price Range
₹0–500 | Free printable versions fully adequate for home use
DIY Alternative (₹0)
Notebook; tally marks; 5-field daily log sheet: Date / Episodes / Antecedent / Alternative Used / Notes
Why It Matters
After 1–2 weeks of tracking, you will know: what time of day, what settings, what triggers. This is your functional assessment in progress.

Act II — Safety
Before you execute any protocol for self-hitting — read this card completely.
🔴 RED — Do Not Proceed
Seek medical evaluation first if: self-hitting is new onset and sudden (may indicate pain); visible injury — bruising, swelling, cuts, eye/head trauma; head-banging against hard surfaces with significant force; child expresses wanting to hurt themselves; any signs of illness, fever, or apparent pain.
🟡 AMBER — Modify & Consult
Multiple forms of self-injury simultaneously; hitting that increases despite basic alternatives; complete absence of any communication system; self-hitting is daily and significantly interfering; child is younger than 18 months.
🟢 GREEN — Proceed
Medical causes ruled out; child is medically stable; hitting is concerning but not causing significant injury; you have completed a basic functional observation; you have one or more of the 9 materials available.

STOP IF YOU SEE: Child becomes more agitated when given alternatives | Hitting intensity escalates during your response | Child develops new forms of self-injury when hitting is blocked. Weighted items: ~10% of body weight max. Compression: snug, not restrictive of breathing or circulation.
Act II — Space Setup
Spatial setup is therapeutic infrastructure. 80% of session failures begin before the session starts.
Key Setup Principles
  1. Alternatives must be visible — the child cannot use what they cannot see or access
  1. Safe hitting targets must be near where hitting normally occurs — across the room doesn't work
  1. Calming corner must be pre-established — not set up during crisis
  1. Communication system must be mounted/accessible in the zone where hitting typically happens
  1. Parent position: same level as child, calm, not hovering
Environmental Checklist
  • Hard walls in head-impact range padded or cushioned
  • Floor in impact zones has mat or rug
  • Sharp furniture corners covered
  • Preferred hitting alternative within arm's reach
  • Communication cards/board visible and accessible
  • Calm-down corner pre-established with calming tools
  • Lighting: soft, not harsh fluorescent
  • Sound: reduced background noise
Your space contains a Calm Corner (weighted blanket + calming tools), a Safe Hitting Zone (hitting pillow + crash pad area), and a Materials Station (all 9 alternatives within visual range of child). Remove hard surfaces at head height. Remove triggering objects. Keep it clean and simple.

Act III — Step 1
Step 1 of 6
The Invitation
Introduce ONE alternative material with no demand, no pressure, no expectations. The child is not required to use it. You are simply placing it in their world.
"Hey [child's name], look what I have here. This is your [hitting pillow / squeeze blanket / deep pressure vest]. It's here whenever you want it." — Then put it down. Step back. Do NOT push.
Body Language
  • Get to the child's physical level
  • Soft voice, neutral tone
  • No urgency, no anxiety in your posture
  • Do not make eye contact if it increases pressure for your child
Reading the Response
Acceptance cues: Looks at material; moves toward it; touches it briefly; picks it up
Resistance cues: Moves away; throws or rejects material; ignores completely → try a different material tomorrow; this one may not match their sensory profile
Timing: 30–60 seconds for the invitation phase. Do not extend it. Plant the seed and step back.
Act III — Step 2
Step 2 of 6
The Engagement
The child has shown some awareness of the material. Now gently demonstrate its use — not as instruction, as modeling. You use it first.
For Deep Pressure Tools
Wrap yourself in the blanket briefly. Say: "Mm, this feels good and heavy." Then offer it again to the child.
For Safe Hitting Alternative
Hit the pillow yourself — lightly. Say: "This is our hitting place." Point to it simply. No drama, no urgency.
For Communication Cards
Hold up the "HELP" card. Model using it: "When I need help, I show this." Place the card near where hitting typically happens.
For Emotional Charts
Point to the "frustrated" face. Say: "This one is frustrated. Like when things are hard." No quiz. No demand. Simply name it.

Reinforcement Cue: The moment the child touches the material — ANY contact — provide immediate, specific praise: "Yes! You touched it!" This is the reinforcement that builds the pathway. Timing: 1–3 minutes.
Act III — Step 3
Step 3 of 6
The Therapeutic Action
This is the active ingredient. The child uses the alternative material in place of or alongside the self-hitting urge. This does not happen on demand — it happens through availability and modeling over repeated sessions.
Proactive (Every 1–2 Hours)
Offer deep pressure input throughout the day: firm squeezes, "sandwich" between cushions, weighted blanket wrap for 5–10 minutes. Fill the proprioceptive need BEFORE it builds to hitting.
Reactive (Pre-Hitting Signal)
Move the hitting pillow or crash pad into the child's space immediately: "Here's your hitting pillow. This is where we hit." For communicative function: physically MODEL the communication alternative together.
Co-Regulate (Emotional Escalation)
Move to the calm-down corner together. Name the emotion on the chart. Offer deep pressure. Sit alongside. Do NOT demand. Simply be present with the tools available.
Child Response
Your Move
Child uses alternative
Reinforce immediately — "Yes! You used it!"
Uses alternative AFTER hitting
Still reinforce — hitting is losing its functional efficiency
Escalates when offered alternative
Wrong material or timing — record and adjust

Act III — Step 5
Step 5 of 6
Reinforce & Celebrate
Behavior that is reinforced increases. When your child uses a safe alternative instead of self-hitting — or even approaches the alternative — that behavior MUST be reinforced immediately, specifically, and enthusiastically. Timing: within 3 seconds of the desired behavior. Not after the session. Not "later." Now.
Verbal Praise
"YES! You squeezed the pillow! That's exactly right!" | "You used your HELP card! I'm so proud of you!" | "You went to your calm corner! That's what we do!"
Sticker Chart
1800+ Reward Stickers ₹364 | Amazon — token economy with strong evidence base in autism intervention
Reward Jar
Rosette Reward Jar ₹589 | Amazon — preferred activities and small tangibles for alternative behavior reinforcement
Preferred Sensory Input
Deep pressure hug, swing time, preferred activity, brief preferred screen time — contingent and time-limited

Critical Rule: If your child communicates "break" or "help" using their system — honor it IMMEDIATELY. Every time you fail to respond to communication, you teach them that hitting is the more reliable language. Celebrate the attempt, not just success — in early stages, reinforce ANY approximation.
Act III — Step 6
Step 6 of 6
The Cool-Down
No session — and no behavioral crisis response — ends abruptly. The transition back to baseline is as therapeutic as the intervention itself. A rushed ending creates post-session dysregulation that looks like a "new" problem.
Two-Minute Warning
"Two more [squeezes / hits on the pillow / breaths], then all done." Give the warning before ending.
Visual Timer
If available, show the timer counting down (1–2 minutes). Time Timer, hourglass timers, apps — Search Amazon.in: "visual timer autism child"
One Calming Input
Weighted blanket for 3 minutes, calming music, or slow rocking. One input only — keep it predictable.
Material Put-Away Ritual
Child participates if able — "Let's put the pillow back in its place." This builds the end-of-session association.
Transition Cue + Positive Closure
"All done [activity]. Now we're going to [next activity]." Then: "You did really well today." Brief, warm, complete.

If Child Resists Ending: Offer ONE more interaction with the material, then use the visual timer. Do NOT abruptly remove materials — fading is smoother than removal. Return control: "You can put it away when you're ready."

Act III — Troubleshoot
Most sessions don't go perfectly. The technique needs adjustment, not you.
Problem 1: Child rejected every material
Why: Materials may not match the function. If hitting is communicative, proprioceptive tools won't resolve it until communication tools are in place. Try: Go back to observation — what function does hitting serve? Start with the functional match.
Problem 2: Child hit then used the alternative
Why: This is actually early progress — the alternative is becoming part of the sequence. Try: Reinforce the alternative use enthusiastically even when it follows hitting. Over time, it will move earlier in the sequence.
Problem 3: Hitting got WORSE after starting
Why: Extinction burst — the old behavior intensifying briefly when it stops working as reliably. This is a sign the function was correctly identified. Try: Stay consistent. Do not capitulate to escalation. Honor communication alternatives immediately.
Problem 4: Can't figure out the function
Why: Many children have multi-function SIB — hitting serves different functions in different contexts. Try: Use ABC tracking (Card 20) for 1–2 weeks. Contact 9100 181 181 for functional behavior assessment support.
Problem 5: Hitting pillow isn't working for head-hitting
Why: Impact sensation to head is different from hand impact. Try: Protective helmet while working on alternatives; ensure hitting pillow is accessible exactly where head-banging occurs; add a crash pad for full-body impact.

Session Abandonment Is Not Failure — It's Data: If today's session had to be abandoned due to dysregulation: record what triggered the abandonment. That trigger is your next intervention target.
Act III — Adapt
No two children are identical. Your protocol should fit your child, not the other way around.
Sensory Profile Variations
For the Proprioceptive SEEKER (craves intense input): Heavy work protocol: carrying groceries, pushing chairs, wall push-ups, weighted vest throughout the day. Crash pad diving; deep pressure squeeze; joint compression. Strong, firm hitting pillow.
For the Overloaded/AVOIDER (hitting to escape overwhelming input): Environment modification first: reduce sensory load (noise, lighting, crowds). Calming tools as the primary material. Communication system for "too much / need break." Gradual desensitization through OT-guided sensory diet.
Age-Based Modifications
Ages 2–4
Focus on ONE material only. Proactive sensory diet. Heavy play. Communication is mostly caregiver-modeled. Keep sessions under 5 minutes.
Ages 5–8
Introduce emotion charts. Build communication system. Begin child-led selection of alternatives. Sessions 10 minutes.
Ages 9–12
Self-monitoring tools. Data co-collection with child. Self-regulation plans. Body awareness training. Child becomes a partner in the process.
Act IV — Progress
Weeks 1–2: Laying the Foundation
Weeks 1–2 are not about stopping. They're about starting to understand. The neural pathway being built has not yet been used. You are laying the foundation — and the absence of dramatic change is not the absence of change.
15%
Progress at Week 2
Foundation established — tolerance and antecedent identification in progress
What You Will Likely See
Material Acknowledgment
Child acknowledges the existence of the alternative materials — even if not using them. Any awareness is progress.
Episode Duration Shifts
Some reduction in episode duration (even if frequency is unchanged). A 10-minute episode that becomes 7 minutes — that is progress.
Antecedent Patterns Emerge
You have identified 2–3 consistent antecedents from your tracking data. One material shows more acceptance than others.

Parent Emotional Preparation: You may feel discouraged in weeks 1–2. That is normal. Trust the process. Document everything. The data you collect now is the foundation for everything that follows.
Act IV — Weeks 3–4
Weeks 3–4: Neural Pathways Are Forming
You'll see it in these specific signs. The new pathway is beginning to compete with the old one — and the competition is visible in behavior.
40%
Progress at Week 4
Consolidation — prompted use before hitting, episode frequency measurably reducing
Prompted Use Before Hitting
Child uses alternative material IN RESPONSE to a prompt — before hitting, not after. This is the consolidation indicator that matters most.
Independent Calm Corner
Child approaches the calm corner independently in 1 out of every 5 escalations. The internal regulation system is beginning to activate.
Predictable Antecedents
You can predict 60–70% of episodes from antecedent patterns. You respond to pre-hitting signals before they escalate.
The Pause
Your child begins to "pause" at the edge of a hitting episode — even for 2 seconds. That pause is the new pathway competing with the old one. It will get longer.

Parent Milestone: You are likely more confident. You respond to pre-hitting signals before they escalate. Your regulation has improved because you have a plan. That is a clinical outcome too.
Act IV — Weeks 5–8
Weeks 5–8: Mastery Is the Presence of Alternatives
75%
Progress at Week 8
Mastery emerging — spontaneous alternative use, measurable frequency reduction, generalization beginning
Indicator
Mastery Threshold
Alternative material use
Spontaneous (without prompt) in ≥3 of 5 escalation situations
Hitting frequency
≥50% reduction from baseline
Communication
Child initiates "help/break/want" in 3+ contexts
Recovery time
From peak dysregulation to calm in <10 min vs. baseline
Generalization
Alternative use appearing in at least 2 settings

Mastery Badge Criteria: ✅ Child independently selects a safe alternative in majority of pre-hitting moments ✅ Family confidently executes the response protocol ✅ At least one setting shows significant behavioral change ✅ Communication system is functional for at least 3 key needs
Act IV — Celebrate
You did this. Your child grew because you showed up — every day, every session.
You started this journey watching your child use their own body as the only tool they had. Over 5–8 weeks, you gave them somewhere else for it to go. That is extraordinary clinical parenting.
What You Did
  • Learned the neuroscience and stopped seeing this as defiance
  • Set up a safe environment before each session
  • Offered alternatives when your instinct was to stop the hitting
  • Collected data when every session felt like chaos
  • Stayed consistent through the extinction burst
Family Celebration Idea
Create a "New Tools" celebration for your child — not for stopping the hitting, but for learning a new skill. "You learned to use the pillow / the blanket / the card. That is STRONG."
Journal Prompt
Document this milestone: What was the first time your child independently chose the alternative? What did it look like? Write it down. Photograph it. This is the before-and-after that matters.
Act IV — Red Flags
Even in the progress zone — these signs mean pause and call.
🔴 Hitting Intensity Increasing
Not decreasing after 4+ weeks of consistent protocol implementation
🔴 New Forms of Self-Injury
Head-banging, biting, or scratching emerging as hitting decreases — behavior substitution, not resolution
🔴 Visible Injuries
Bruising, swelling, eye trauma, or skin breakdown not resolving
🔴 School Escalation
School reporting escalation in self-hitting even as home improves — requires coordinated assessment
Escalation Pathway

"If something feels wrong — if the hitting is changing in a way that concerns you — pause the protocol and call 9100 181 181. Our helpline is available 24×7, in 16+ languages. You do not have to navigate this alone."

Act V — Community
Real families. Real outcomes. Documented through GPT-OS®.
Arjun, Age 5 — Proprioceptive Seeking
Before: Hit himself dozens of times per day. Triggers: transitions, homework, loud environments. Injury marks were frequent.
Intervention: OT identified proprioceptive-seeking function. Weighted vest introduced proactively. Safe hitting pillow at each transition point.
After 8 weeks: 70% frequency reduction. Arjun reaches for his vest independently before known triggers.
Priya, Age 7 — Communicative SIB
Before: Hit her head and face when unable to communicate. No functional language. Hitting was her loudest communication tool.
Intervention: SLP-led AAC. Simple PECS board: HELP / BREAK / WANT / STOP. Every communicative use honored immediately.
After 6 weeks: 85% reduction. 12-symbol board. "She wasn't hitting me to hurt herself. She was screaming with the only language she had."
Rohan, Age 4 — Emotional Regulation
Before: Hit himself during frustration, disappointment, excitement. Hitting was emotional release.
Intervention: Emotion chart + calm corner + deep pressure co-regulation.
After 10 weeks: Points to "frustrated" face. Moves to calm corner with parent. "He has options now. He's not just a storm. He has an eye in the storm."
